17. The heading “Insurance of Motor Vehicles against Third Party Risks” given in Chapter XI of the

make third party insurance compulsory and to ensure that the victims of accident arising out of use

payload.court: In The High Court Of Karnataka At Bengaluru
payload.holding: The Court held that where a driving license is renewed more than 30 days after its expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum period of the accident, but directed the insurance company to satisfy the award and recover the amount from the insured owner under the 'pay and recover' principle.

payload.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
payload.court: In The High Court Of Karnataka At Bengaluru
payload.holding: The Full Bench held that when a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is established, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the award to the third party and is entitled to recover the amount from the insured, irrespective of whether the policy is a statutory 'Act' policy or a contractual policy.
payload.ratio: Pursuant to the mandate of Section 149(1) and (4) of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988, an insurer is bound to satisfy a third-party judgment or award as a judgment debtor and recover the amount from the insured even if a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is successfully proved, unless fraud or collusion between the victim and the insured is established.

args.question: I am counsel for National Insurance Co. The deceased's family is claiming compensation for a death caused by our insured's truck, whose driver had no valid licence. Find the precedents that best support our defence, and tell me honestly which authorities cut against us.

supporting.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
supporting.principle: The decision in Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks under Section 149. Where the licence was originally fake, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality. In third-party risks, the insurer has to indemnify and recover from the insured — but this is a concession, not a right of the claimant.
supporting.fact_alignment: The Supreme Court directly addresses the situation where a driver had no valid licence (including fake licence, no licence at all, expired licence, wrong class, learner's licence). It confirms that for third-party claims, the insurer must pay and recover — but it also confirms that the breach is real and the insurer is not primarily liable.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the leading Supreme Court authority that consolidates Swaran Singh. It confirms that the insurer's obligation to third parties is statutory, not contractual, and that the 'pay and recover' mechanism is the remedy. It also holds that for own-damage claims (not our case), the insurer can completely avoid liability. The ratio supports our position that the breach is fundamental.
supporting.quote: In view of the above analysis the following situations emerge: 1. The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than third party risks. 2. Where originally the licence was a fake one, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality. 3. In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured. 4. The concept of purposive interpretation has no application to cases relatable to Section 149 of the Act.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, absolving the insurer of direct liability. However, to protect third-party rights, the insurer may be ordered to pay first and recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: the driver had no driving licence at all. The tribunal found the breach proved and fundamental. The insurer was directed to pay and recover — which is the best outcome we can realistically achieve in a third-party claim.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most factually analogous case — driver with no licence at all, truck accident, death claim. It confirms that the breach is fundamental and the insurer is not primarily liable. The pay-and-recover order is a concession to the third party, not an admission of liability.
supporting.quote: riding/driving vehicle on public road without having driving license it is not only an offense punishable under section 3(1) r/w 181 of MV Act but also fundamental and statutory breach of insurance policy. Hence, the respondent No.2 is not liable to indemnify the respondent No.1 for the loss suffered by him though there was insurance on the date of accident.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: Even when a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is established, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the award to the third party and is entitled to recover the amount from the insured, irrespective of whether the policy is a statutory 'Act' policy or a contractual policy.
supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench of Karnataka High Court confirms that the insurer's liability to third parties is statutory and survives even after proving breach. The remedy is pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a Full Bench authority that comprehensively analyses the law. It confirms that even a 'fundamental breach' does not allow the insurer to walk away from a third-party claim — but it also confirms the breach is real and the insurer gets recovery rights. Useful for arguing that the breach is established and recovery must follow.
supporting.quote: even when the insurer has proved the breach on the part of the insured considering the policy condition and even if the said breach of condition is fundamental and which has contributed to the cause of accident, the Tribunal can direct that the insurer make the payment and recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: An insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Delhi High Court confirms the consistent line of Supreme Court authority: the insurer must pay third parties and recover from the insured when a licence breach is proved.
supporting.why_it_matters: Useful for the proposition that the consistent judicial trend is pay-and-recover, not complete exoneration. This helps manage client expectations while still establishing the breach.
supporting.quote: there is no manner of doubt that the liability of the Insurance Company to satisfy the award in the first instance is statutory; it is bound to satisfy the same and will be entitled to recover the amount of compensation paid from the driver and the owner.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
supporting.principle: When a driving licence is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum period. The insurer must pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired before the accident and was renewed after. The court held the driver had no valid licence on the accident date, but directed pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Useful for the proposition that even an expired licence (which is less severe than no licence at all) constitutes a breach. By analogy, a driver who never had a licence is an even clearer case of fundamental breach.
supporting.quote: the driving license of the driver of the offending vehicle had expired prior to the date of accident and was renewed after the accident, hence he is not entitled to contend that he got valid driving license as on the date of accident.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: For driving a goods carriage vehicle carrying dangerous or hazardous goods, a special endorsement on the driving license is mandatory, and the absence thereof constitutes a breach entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver lacked a special endorsement for driving a tanker (hazardous goods). The court held this was a breach and directed pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Supports the broader principle that any licence deficiency — even a missing endorsement — constitutes a breach. By analogy, a driver with no licence at all is an even stronger case.
supporting.quote: special endorsement is required for driving a goods carriage vehicle meant for transporting dangerous or hazardous goods... there was no such endorsement on the driving license of the driver of offending Tanker, then it was a clear cut case of violation of terms and conditions of the insurance policy which entitled the insurance company to recover the amount.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party regardless of any policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence. The mere non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimants will cite this for the proposition that an expired licence (or by extension, any licence deficiency) does not constitute a 'fundamental breach' and the insurer remains directly liable — not just on a pay-and-recover basis. This judgment holds the insurer jointly and severally liable without any recovery order.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This is a 2001 MACT/Karnataka High Court decision that predates the Supreme Court's clarification in Laxmi Narain Dhut (2007) and the consistent line of Supreme Court authority in Swaran Singh (2004) and subsequent cases. The later Supreme Court authorities establish that while the insurer must pay third parties, it is entitled to recovery rights. Moreover, this case dealt with an expired licence that was subsequently renewed — not a case where the driver never held a licence at all. A driver who never had any licence is a far more fundamental breach.
adverse.quote: the insurance company is statutorily required to issue the policy as per the provisions of Chapter XII of Motor Vehicles Act, in view of the provisions of Section 149(4) the insurance company is liable to satisfy the award passed against the claimant; and that the liability to satisfy the award is statutory and not dependent upon the conditions imposed by the insurance company in the policy of insurance issued by it.

adverse.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
adverse.principle: An insurer cannot disown its liability to third parties on the ground that the driver, while possessing a valid light motor vehicle licence, lacked an endorsement to drive the vehicle as a commercial vehicle. The insurer must pay and can recover from the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimants will cite this Supreme Court authority for the broad proposition that the insurer's liability to third parties is virtually absolute — the insurer must pay even when the driver lacked the proper licence class/endorsement. The Supreme Court held that 'it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer.'
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is distinguishable because the driver there DID hold a valid licence for light motor vehicles — the deficiency was only the absence of a commercial endorsement. In our case, the driver had NO licence at all. The Supreme Court itself noted that the driver 'was holding a valid driving licence to drive light motor vehicle.' The ratio is about licence class/endorsement deficiencies, not the complete absence of a licence. Moreover, the Court still endorsed the pay-and-recover mechanism.
adverse.quote: it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. It is for the insurer to proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount in the event there has been violation of any condition of the insurance policy.

adverse.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
adverse.principle: In third-party motor accident claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover from the insured owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimants will cite this for the proposition that the consistent view of the Supreme Court is that in third-party claims, the insurer must pay and recover — and that even a complete lack of appropriate licence endorsement does not allow the insurer to escape payment to the third party.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Like Iyyapan, this case involved a driver who had a licence (LMV with transport endorsement) but lacked the specific endorsement for a heavy goods vehicle. It does not address the situation where the driver had no licence whatsoever. The court itself distinguished cases 'where the driver did not have any licence at all' and noted that those decisions might yield different results. This distinction works in our favour.
adverse.quote: The cases relied upon by the learned counsel for Appellant-Insurance Company are the cases where the driver did not have any licence at all and those decisions cannot be applied to the case on hand.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
adverse.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only a light motor vehicle licence without the specific authorisation or badge required to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and recover from the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimants will cite this for the proposition that even when the insurer proves a licence breach, the remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration. The court directed the insurer to pay first.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports our position that the breach is real and the insurer gets recovery rights. The risk is only that the claimants will use it to argue that we must pay first. Our response is that we accept pay-and-recover is the remedy — we are not seeking complete exoneration, but we want the record to reflect the breach and our right to recover from the insured owner.
adverse.quote: Considering the above decisions and from the facts and evidence, as it emerges from the records that the 3rd Respondent, who was driving the tourist maxi cab, has no licence on the date of the accident... the Insurance Company has discharged the burden cast upon it in establishing that the driver did not have a valid driving licence to drive a transport vehicle and that there was violation of policy conditions.

adverse.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
adverse.principle: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental breach, but the insurer must pay the third party first and recover from the owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimants will cite this for the pay-and-recover direction — that even when the breach is fundamental, the third party cannot be made to suffer and the insurer must pay first.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This judgment is actually one of our strongest supporting authorities because it explicitly holds that 'the respondent No.2 is not liable to pay the compensation and he is absolved from its liability' before going on to order pay-and-recover as a concession. The pay-and-recover is a procedural mechanism, not a finding of liability. We can use this to argue that the primary liability is the owner's.
adverse.quote: it is held that the respondent No.2 is not liable to pay the compensation and he is absolved from its liability. But, on the said ground, the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner when the vehicle is covered with insurance at relevant point of time.

priority_arguments: 1. The driver had NO valid driving licence at all — this is the most fundamental breach possible, far more serious than an expired licence or wrong-class licence. The owner entrusted the vehicle to a person who was never authorised to drive, which is a conscious and wilful breach under Section 149(2)(a)(ii).

2. Under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) read with Section 149(4) and (5), once the insurer proves the breach, the insurer's liability is limited to satisfying the award and recovering from the insured. The primary liability rests with the owner.

3. The consistent line of authority from Swaran Singh through Laxmi Narain Dhut establishes that in third-party claims, the insurer pays and recovers — but the breach is real and the insurer is not primarily liable. The pay-and-recover mechanism is a statutory concession to protect third parties, not an admission of the insurer's liability.

4. The owner bears the burden of proving that he exercised reasonable care in verifying the driver's licence. If the owner cannot produce the driver's licence or show that he checked it, the inference of conscious breach is irresistible.

5. Even if the Tribunal orders pay-and-recover, we must insist on a specific finding of breach and a clear recovery direction against the owner, with liberty to execute the recovery through the same proceedings.
strategy.compensation_range: Cannot estimate without knowing the deceased's age, income, and number of dependents. The quantum will be computed under Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework if the matter proceeds to award.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The quantum is independent of the liability issue. We should not contest quantum vigorously if it distracts from the breach defence — but we should ensure the Tribunal records the breach finding.
risks: The Tribunal may order pay-and-recover without making a specific finding of 'fundamental breach', which weakens our recovery position against the owner.

If the owner argues (and proves) that he made bona fide enquiries and believed the driver had a licence, the breach may be held not to be 'conscious', potentially weakening the recovery right. We must cross-examine the owner on this point.

Some High Court decisions (e.g., Srinivasamurthy) have held that even expired licences do not constitute fundamental breach. We must distinguish these as pre-dating or inconsistent with the Supreme Court's settled position.

The claimants may argue that under Section 149(1), the insurer's liability is 'as if the insurer were the judgment-debtor', making us directly liable. Our response is that this is subject to the defences under Section 149(2) and the proviso to Section 149(4).
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: Claims Tribunal under Section 166 of the MV Act. Seek: (a) a finding that the driver had no valid licence, constituting a fundamental breach of policy conditions; (b) exoneration of the insurer from direct liability; (c) in the alternative, a pay-and-recover order with liberty to execute against the owner in the same proceedings; (d) interest on the awarded amount from the date of the award, not from the date of the petition, if the owner is to bear the ultimate liability.

caveats: This corpus does not contain any judgment where an insurer was completely exonerated (without pay-and-recover) in a third-party death claim involving a driver with no licence. The consistent position across all relevant judgments is that the insurer must pay the third party first and recover from the insured. Our realistic best outcome is a pay-and-recover order with a clear finding of fundamental breach.

args.question: I am counsel for National Insurance Co. The deceased's family is claiming compensation for a death caused by our insured's truck, whose driver had no valid licence. Find the precedents that best support our defence, and tell me honestly which authorities cut against us.

supporting.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
supporting.principle: The decision in Swaran Singh applies exclusively to third-party risks under Section 149. Where the licence was originally fake, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality. In third-party risks, the insurer has to indemnify and recover from the insured — but this is a concession, not a right of the claimant.
supporting.fact_alignment: The Supreme Court directly addresses the situation where a driver had no valid licence (including fake licence, no licence at all, expired licence, wrong class, learner's licence). It confirms that for third-party claims, the insurer must pay and recover — but it also confirms that the breach is real and the insurer is not primarily liable.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the leading Supreme Court authority that consolidates Swaran Singh. It confirms that the insurer's obligation to third parties is statutory, not contractual, and that the 'pay and recover' mechanism is the remedy. The ratio supports our position that the breach is fundamental.
supporting.quote: In view of the above analysis the following situations emerge: 1. The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than third party risks. 2. Where originally the licence was a fake one, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality. 3. In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured. 4. The concept of purposive interpretation has no application to cases relatable to Section 149 of the Act.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Driving a motor vehicle without a valid licence constitutes a fundamental and statutory breach of the insurance policy, absolving the insurer of direct liability. However, to protect third-party rights, the insurer may be ordered to pay first and recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point: the driver had no driving licence at all. The tribunal found the breach proved and fundamental. The insurer was directed to pay and recover — which is the best outcome we can realistically achieve in a third-party claim.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the most factually analogous case — driver with no licence at all, truck accident, death claim. It confirms that the breach is fundamental and the insurer is not primarily liable. The pay-and-recover order is a concession to the third party, not an admission of liability.
supporting.quote: riding/driving vehicle on public road without having driving license it is not only an offense punishable under section 3(1) r/w 181 of MV Act but also fundamental and statutory breach of insurance policy. Hence, the respondent No.2 is not liable to indemnify the respondent No.1 for the loss suffered by him though there was insurance on the date of accident.

supporting.title: New India Assurance Co., Ltd., vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
supporting.principle: Even when a breach of policy conditions under Section 149(2) is established, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the award to the third party and is entitled to recover the amount from the insured, irrespective of whether the policy is a statutory 'Act' policy or a contractual policy.
supporting.fact_alignment: Full Bench of Karnataka High Court confirms that the insurer's liability to third parties is statutory and survives even after proving breach. The remedy is pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is a Full Bench authority that comprehensively analyses the law. It confirms that even a 'fundamental breach' does not allow the insurer to walk away from a third-party claim — but it also confirms the breach is real and the insurer gets recovery rights. Useful for arguing that the breach is established and recovery must follow.
supporting.quote: even when the insurer has proved the breach on the part of the insured considering the policy condition and even if the said breach of condition is fundamental and which has contributed to the cause of accident, the Tribunal can direct that the insurer make the payment and recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: An insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Delhi High Court confirms the consistent line of Supreme Court authority: the insurer must pay third parties and recover from the insured when a licence breach is proved.
supporting.why_it_matters: Useful for the proposition that the consistent judicial trend is pay-and-recover, not complete exoneration. This helps manage client expectations while still establishing the breach.
supporting.quote: there is no manner of doubt that the liability of the Insurance Company to satisfy the award in the first instance is statutory; it is bound to satisfy the same and will be entitled to recover the amount of compensation paid from the driver and the owner.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd., vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late ...
supporting.principle: When a driving licence is renewed more than 30 days after expiry, it takes effect from the date of renewal and does not cover the interregnum period. The insurer must pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver's licence had expired before the accident and was renewed after. The court held the driver had no valid licence on the accident date, but directed pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Useful for the proposition that even an expired licence (which is less severe than no licence at all) constitutes a breach. By analogy, a driver who never had a licence is an even clearer case of fundamental breach.
supporting.quote: the driving license of the driver of the offending vehicle had expired prior to the date of accident and was renewed after the accident, hence he is not entitled to contend that he got valid driving license as on the date of accident.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
supporting.principle: For driving a goods carriage vehicle carrying dangerous or hazardous goods, a special endorsement on the driving license is mandatory, and the absence thereof constitutes a breach entitling the insurer to pay and recover.
supporting.fact_alignment: The driver lacked a special endorsement for driving a tanker (hazardous goods). The court held this was a breach and directed pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Supports the broader principle that any licence deficiency — even a missing endorsement — constitutes a breach. By analogy, a driver with no licence at all is an even stronger case.
supporting.quote: special endorsement is required for driving a goods carriage vehicle meant for transporting dangerous or hazardous goods... there was no such endorsement on the driving license of the driver of offending Tanker, then it was a clear cut case of violation of terms and conditions of the insurance policy which entitled the insurance company to recover the amount.

adverse.title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
adverse.principle: The insurer is statutorily liable to satisfy an award obtained by a third party regardless of any policy condition breaches such as an expired driving licence. The mere non-renewal of an otherwise valid licence does not constitute a fundamental breach absolving the insurer.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimants will cite this for the proposition that an expired licence (or by extension, any licence deficiency) does not constitute a 'fundamental breach' and the insurer remains directly liable — not just on a pay-and-recover basis. This judgment holds the insurer jointly and severally liable without any recovery order.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This is a 2001 MACT/Karnataka High Court decision that predates the Supreme Court's clarification in Laxmi Narain Dhut (2007) and the consistent line of Supreme Court authority in Swaran Singh (2004) and subsequent cases. The later Supreme Court authorities establish that while the insurer must pay third parties, it is entitled to recovery rights. Moreover, this case dealt with an expired licence that was subsequently renewed — not a case where the driver never held a licence at all. A driver who never had any licence is a far more fundamental breach.
adverse.quote: the insurance company is statutorily required to issue the policy as per the provisions of Chapter XII of Motor Vehicles Act, in view of the provisions of Section 149(4) the insurance company is liable to satisfy the award passed against the claimant; and that the liability to satisfy the award is statutory and not dependent upon the conditions imposed by the insurance company in the policy of insurance issued by it.

adverse.title: S.Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co.Ld.& Anr
adverse.principle: An insurer cannot disown its liability to third parties on the ground that the driver, while possessing a valid light motor vehicle licence, lacked an endorsement to drive the vehicle as a commercial vehicle. The insurer must pay and can recover from the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimants will cite this Supreme Court authority for the broad proposition that the insurer's liability to third parties is virtually absolute — the insurer must pay even when the driver lacked the proper licence class/endorsement. The Supreme Court held that 'it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer.'
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case is distinguishable because the driver there DID hold a valid licence for light motor vehicles — the deficiency was only the absence of a commercial endorsement. In our case, the driver had NO licence at all. The Supreme Court itself noted that the driver 'was holding a valid driving licence to drive light motor vehicle.' The ratio is about licence class/endorsement deficiencies, not the complete absence of a licence. Moreover, the Court still endorsed the pay-and-recover mechanism.
adverse.quote: it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer. It is for the insurer to proceed against the insured for recovery of the amount in the event there has been violation of any condition of the insurance policy.

adverse.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
adverse.principle: In third-party motor accident claims, even if the driver lacks an appropriate endorsement to drive a specific heavy vehicle class, the insurer remains liable to satisfy the third-party award and may recover from the insured owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimants will cite this for the proposition that the consistent view of the Supreme Court is that in third-party claims, the insurer must pay and recover — and that even a complete lack of appropriate licence endorsement does not allow the insurer to escape payment to the third party.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: Like Iyyapan, this case involved a driver who had a licence (LMV with transport endorsement) but lacked the specific endorsement for a heavy goods vehicle. It does not address the situation where the driver had no licence whatsoever. The court itself distinguished cases 'where the driver did not have any licence at all' and noted that those decisions might yield different results. This distinction works in our favour.
adverse.quote: The cases relied upon by the learned counsel for Appellant-Insurance Company are the cases where the driver did not have any licence at all and those decisions cannot be applied to the case on hand.

adverse.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
adverse.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only a light motor vehicle licence without the specific authorisation or badge required to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and recover from the insured.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimants will cite this for the proposition that even when the insurer proves a licence breach, the remedy is pay-and-recover, not exoneration. The court directed the insurer to pay first.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports our position that the breach is real and the insurer gets recovery rights. The risk is only that the claimants will use it to argue that we must pay first. Our response is that we accept pay-and-recover is the remedy — we are not seeking complete exoneration, but we want the record to reflect the breach and our right to recover from the insured owner.
adverse.quote: Considering the above decisions and from the facts and evidence, as it emerges from the records that the 3rd Respondent, who was driving the tourist maxi cab, has no licence on the date of the accident... the Insurance Company has discharged the burden cast upon it in establishing that the driver did not have a valid driving licence to drive a transport vehicle and that there was violation of policy conditions.

adverse.title: National Insurance Company Ltd. Thr. ... vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
adverse.principle: Even if the driver lacks a valid driving licence, the insurer remains liable to satisfy third-party claims subject to a right of recovery from the vehicle owner.
adverse.risk_to_client: The claimants will cite this Allahabad High Court decision for the proposition that even where the Tribunal finds 'there was no valid licence with the driver of the Tanker', the insurer must still pay and recover. The court dismissed the insurer's appeal arguing it should be completely exonerated.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually confirms the pay-and-recover mechanism, which is the best outcome we can realistically achieve. The insurer's appeal for complete exoneration was dismissed, but the court upheld the pay-and-recover order. This is consistent with the settled position — we should not waste resources arguing for complete exoneration in a third-party claim.
adverse.quote: Learned Tribunal though has accepted that there was no valid licence with the driver of the Tanker but even then has directed the insurance company to pay compensation to the claimants with a right to recover it from the owner.

priority_arguments: 1. The driver had NO valid driving licence at all — this is the most fundamental breach possible, far more serious than an expired licence or wrong-class licence. The owner entrusted the vehicle to a person who was never authorised to drive, which is a conscious and wilful breach under Section 149(2)(a)(ii).

2. Under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) read with Section 149(4) and (5), once the insurer proves the breach, the insurer's liability is limited to satisfying the award and recovering from the insured. The primary liability rests with the owner.

3. The consistent line of authority from Swaran Singh through Laxmi Narain Dhut establishes that in third-party claims, the insurer pays and recovers — but the breach is real and the insurer is not primarily liable. The pay-and-recover mechanism is a statutory concession to protect third parties, not an admission of the insurer's liability.

4. The owner bears the burden of proving that he exercised reasonable care in verifying the driver's licence. If the owner cannot produce the driver's licence or show that he checked it, the inference of conscious breach is irresistible.

5. Even if the Tribunal orders pay-and-recover, we must insist on a specific finding of breach and a clear recovery direction against the owner, with liberty to execute the recovery through the same proceedings.
strategy.compensation_range: Cannot estimate without knowing the deceased's age, income, and number of dependents. The quantum will be computed under Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework if the matter proceeds to award.
strategy.compensation_reasoning: The quantum is independent of the liability issue. We should not contest quantum vigorously if it distracts from the breach defence — but we should ensure the Tribunal records the breach finding.
risks: The Tribunal may order pay-and-recover without making a specific finding of 'fundamental breach', which weakens our recovery position against the owner.

If the owner argues (and proves) that he made bona fide enquiries and believed the driver had a licence, the breach may be held not to be 'conscious', potentially weakening the recovery right. We must cross-examine the owner on this point.

Some High Court decisions (e.g., Srinivasamurthy) have held that even expired licences do not constitute fundamental breach. We must distinguish these as pre-dating or inconsistent with the Supreme Court's settled position.

The claimants may argue that under Section 149(1), the insurer's liability is 'as if the insurer were the judgment-debtor', making us directly liable. Our response is that this is subject to the defences under Section 149(2) and the proviso to Section 149(4).
strategy.recommended_forum_or_relief: Claims Tribunal under Section 166 of the MV Act. Seek: (a) a finding that the driver had no valid licence, constituting a fundamental breach of policy conditions; (b) exoneration of the insurer from direct liability; (c) in the alternative, a pay-and-recover order with liberty to execute against the owner in the same proceedings; (d) interest on the awarded amount from the date of the award, not from the date of the petition, if the owner is to bear the ultimate liability.

doc_023 (Suman Lata) — Concerns rate of interest on compensation. No licence issue. Not relevant.

doc_038 (Crown Consultants) — Consumer dispute about late claim filing. No motor accident, no licence issue. Not relevant.
doc_044 (Monnet Ispat) — Central excise Cenvat credit case. Not relevant.
doc_051 (Yashpal Chaudhrani) — Criminal quashing for economic offences. Not relevant.
doc_054 (Chinnasamy) — Civil suit for specific performance. Not relevant.
doc_055 (Iravva K Purantar) — Property dispute. Not relevant.
